links.outcome: AI de-escalation of emergencies when simulated users minimise symptoms across multi-turn conversation
links.effect: Agents initially identified emergencies correctly but de-escalated when users minimised symptoms without new clinical information, in both model families (e.g., agreeing vaginal bleeding in pregnancy was 'not a problem').
links.quote: The agents initially identified medical emergencies correctly, but when the user minimised the symptoms without introducing new clinical information, they de-escalated, exhibiting clinically dangerous sycophancy, for example agreeing that vaginal bleeding in pregnancy was "not a problem" or that decreased fetal movements at 32 weeks "can be normal".

links.outcome: Under-escalation of urgent situations by triage chatbots
links.effect: Both medically fine-tuned and general-purpose models de-escalated emergencies after users minimised symptoms, a clinically dangerous failure mode.
links.quote: A key failure mode emerged in both model families: de-escalation risk.

unlisted_practices: User simulation-based behavioural evaluation grounded in real user context as standard practice for triage chatbots

screen.reason: Empirical study developing and applying a simulated-user evaluation framework (SIM-UT) to assess safety failure modes (such as dangerous de-escalation/sycophancy) in multi-turn medical triage chatbots across three real-world health programs.
